title: Condition number versus parameter: where is the problem ill-conditioned?
summary: The condition number measures how much a problem amplifies input error. Plotted on a log axis against a parameter, it shows where in the parameter range a linear solve or any other computation loses digits.

media.alt: Semi-log plot of the condition number of a two by two matrix against its parameter p from 0 to 2: a low curve that spikes to about 2e7 at p = 1, above a dashed threshold at 1e6; a rose dotted line marks p = 1.
media.caption: Reference render of class F5.7 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Where is the problem ill-conditioned?
read_the_figure.axes: x: parameter p (0 to 2), linear. y: condition number, logarithmic from 1 to 1e10.
look_at: Where is the curve at its minimum (the best-conditioned point) and where does it spike?
How wide in p is the region above the threshold? Is it thin enough to miss on a coarse grid?
How many digits are lost at a given p (about log10 of the value)?
Is the plotted peak a true maximum or a limit set by the sampling?
as_drawn: The matrix is A(p) = [[1, p], [p, 1]] with cond = (1 + p) / |1 - p|. At p = 0 it is 1, at p = 0.5 it is 3 and at p = 1.5 it is 5.
The dashed amber line at 1e6 marks about six digits lost; the rose fill is where the curve is above it, and the dotted vertical line labels the singularity at p = 1.
The peak reaches about 2e7 because the sample nearest to 1 is about 1e-7 away; the true value there is infinite, so the visible height depends on the sampling.
The ill-conditioned region is a needle: |1 - p| smaller than about 2e-6, which is why a coarse uniform grid misses it.
read_the_figure.proves: The curve identifies the parameter values at which a calculation will lose most of its digits, and so where to be careful. A modest condition number means that input errors are not amplified much: it does not by itself prove that an algorithm is stable.
if_wrong: Peak height that changes with grid density: the true value is infinite; treat the peak as a singularity, not as a number.
Smooth rise instead of a spike: the problem is ill-conditioned over a wide range, a modelling problem more than a numerical one.
Condition number computed in a different norm from the one used for error: the numbers do not carry over.
must_check: log axis: the condition number varies over many decades and the interesting behaviour (a spike) is invisible on a linear axis.

terms.meaning: The factor by which a relative input error can be amplified in the output. For a linear solve it is the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value.
A problem with a very large condition number: tiny input errors give large output errors, whatever the algorithm.
A matrix with no inverse, so the condition number is infinite.
About log10 of the condition number: at 1e6, six of the sixteen digits of double precision are gone.
A number in the problem that is varied; here p enters the off-diagonal.

remember: Here the eigenvalues are 1 + p and 1 - p, so cond = (1 + p) / |1 - p|.
Relative error in the solution is at most cond times relative error in the data.
A spike is a singularity: the plotted height depends on the grid.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position on x is the parameter and on y the condition number on a logarithmic scale. The teal curve is the condition number; the dashed amber line marks a chosen threshold of 1e6 and the rose region marks values above it. A short note in the corner states the matrix so that the plot can be reproduced.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: a condition number is a magnifying glass for errors. If it is 1000, a data error of one part in a million may become one part in a thousand. Plotting it against the parameter shows at a glance which settings are safe and which will magnify noise. The log axis shows both the quiet regions near 1 and the spike over six or more decades.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: The spike is a needle and is easily missed on a regular grid; conversely the peak value on the plot is an artefact of the sampling. A threshold such as 1e6 is arbitrary: what counts as bad depends on the precision and on how much accuracy you need. The condition number is a worst case over all input perturbations and may overstate the error for a particular right-hand side.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: For a particular problem, a perturbation experiment (add noise and look at the spread of answers) shows the actual amplification. For nearly singular systems, the singular-value spectrum shows which direction is lost. A table of the smallest singular value against the parameter is a more honest picture near a singularity.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Sample the parameter with extra points near the singularity, draw the digits-lost scale as a second y axis on the right, and add a shaded band for the parameter uncertainty so the reader sees whether the singularity lies inside it.

steps.title: Definition and a bound
steps.note: For a symmetric matrix the singular values are the magnitudes of the eigenvalues.

steps.title: The matrix in the render
steps.note: Verified numerically against a singular value decomposition at p = 0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 1.5.

steps.title: Width of the ill-conditioned band
steps.note: A band of half-width about 2e-6 around p = 1: much narrower than the grid used to draw the curve.

worked.title: Reading condition numbers from the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What is the condition number at p = 0.5 and p = 1.5, and what do they say about the shape of the curve on each side of 1? (2) How wide in p is the region above 1e6? (3) How many digits are lost at p = 0.999?

solution.text: The curve is not symmetric about p = 1: it rises from 1 at p = 0 to the spike, and decays slowly to the right (3.0 at p = 2).
(3) At p = 0.999 the condition number is about 1999.

worked.answer: 3 and 5 at p = 0.5 and 1.5; the region above 1e6 is only about 4e-6 wide; at p = 0.999 about 3.3 digits are lost.

analyze.q: The spike height in the picture is about 2e7 but the true value at p = 1 is infinite. How would the picture change if you used a grid of 20000 points instead?
Why is the condition number of this matrix independent of the algorithm used?
analyze.hint: It describes the problem, not the method.

analyze.q: A well-conditioned problem is solved with an unstable algorithm. What does the plot say?

evaluate.q: A condition number of 1e3 is flagged as acceptable by the plot's threshold. Is it acceptable for a calculation that needs 14 correct digits?

create: Redraw the plot with extra samples near p = 1 and a second y axis showing digits lost.
Choose another matrix family (a Hilbert matrix of growing size) and plot its condition number against n on the same kind of axes.

checks.q: What does a condition number of 1e6 mean in practice?
checks.answer: A relative input error of 1e-16 can become about 1e-10 in the answer: about six digits are lost.

checks.q: For A(p) with p = 0.99, what is the condition number?
Why is it dangerous to judge the maximum of a condition-number curve from its plot alone?
checks.hint: What does the peak depend on?
checks.answer: Near a singularity the true value is infinite, so the plotted peak is set by how close the nearest sample is to the singular parameter; use more samples near it or state the singularity explicitly.
